note: claude-opus-5-5、入力 2988 / 出力 3238 トークン

data.interpretation: From period 5, the KPI makes fairness between companies the main concern. A road-rule change should not shift advantage toward or away from any one company. On-time delivery remains important, but as a secondary requirement. Orders are falling, so absolute delivery counts will drop whatever the rules are. Per-company rates and gaps are therefore more informative than town-wide counts. The closest measurable reading of 'no company gains or loses because of how the road is used' is the spread of company utility (on-time deliveries minus sanctions). That spread is exactly what moved when D1 cut C's utility. On-time performance is kept as a floor and as monitored goals, so fairness cannot be bought by making every company worse.

options.label: Fairness of outcomes first: minimize the utility gap, with an on-time floor

goals.text: Main goal: reduce the difference between the best-off and worst-off company's utility (on-time deliveries minus sanctions).
Monitor: the worst company's on-time rate should not fall.
Monitor: town-wide on-time deliveries should not fall relative to the same-seed baseline.
Monitor: late deliveries should not rise.

guards.text: Every company keeps an on-time rate of at least 0.9. Period 1 measured 0.98 after D1, so this replaces K1's provisional 0.7.

options.note: Closest to the KPI's wording: utility is what a company gains or loses. Risk: utility_gap also reflects differences in order volume and sanctions, not only road use.

options.label: Fairness of service: minimize the on-time rate gap, with an on-time floor

goals.text: Main goal: reduce the difference between the highest and lowest company on-time rates.
Monitor: the utility gap between companies should not widen.
Monitor: town-wide on-time deliveries should not fall.
Monitor: orders left unfinished at period end should not rise.

guards.text: Every company keeps an on-time rate of at least 0.9.

options.note: Rates are normalized by each company's order count, so this is less sensitive to uneven demand in the quiet season. It measures service to customers more than company advantage.

options.label: On-time first, with fairness as a hard limit

goals.text: Main goal: increase town-wide on-time deliveries.
Monitor: the utility gap between companies should not widen.
Monitor: the worst company's on-time rate should not fall.

guards.text: Company on-time rates stay within 0.1 of each other.
Every company keeps an on-time rate of at least 0.9.

options.note: Keeps continuity with K1, treating fairness as a constraint rather than the objective. It underweights the KPI's 'but', and with fewer orders the main goal will show only small, noisy gains.

concerns: The KPI can be read two ways. Fairness can be the objective ('to keep the companies cooperating, no single company should gain or lose'), or a constraint on continuing to maximize on-time delivery ('on-time delivery still matters'). Options 1-2 take the first reading; option 3 takes the second.

utility_gap is a proxy. It measures differences in outcomes, not differences caused by road use. Companies with different order volumes will differ in utility even under perfectly neutral rules. Minimizing the gap could therefore reward rules that handicap a busier company.

Any gap metric can be improved by leveling down, making the better-off companies worse rather than the worse-off better. The on-time floor and the monitored goals are meant to block this. The floor value of 0.9 is my choice based on the 0.98 measured after D1, and the human should confirm it.
In the quiet season, order counts per company are small. Rates and gaps will be noisy across seeds, so improvements may need more seeds before they count as reliable (compare D2's 2 of 5 seeds).

revisit.why: K1 made town-wide on-time deliveries the main goal with a provisional 0.7 floor. The new KPI puts inter-company fairness first, so K1 is superseded. Its provisional floor should also be replaced with a value informed by the measured 0.98.

D1 (block_k 3 → 2) was adopted against B's and C's votes because it raised town-wide on-time delivery. It cut C's utility from 28.8 to 19.0. The new KPI says no company should lose because of how the road is used, so D1's justification no longer holds by itself. C's utility and the utility gap under block_k 2 should be re-measured and compared against reverting or compensating changes.

D3 was an automatic 'no change' judged against on_time_deliveries as the main goal. Under a fairness main goal, candidate amendments might now qualify as improvements, or the baseline might be judged unfair.
Same as D3: this automatic 'no change' was evaluated against the old main goal and should be re-evaluated under the new one.
